request.prompt:
You are clustering code review findings from the same PR. For each PAIR below, decide whether the two findings describe the SAME underlying issue — same root cause in the same code location. Different wording is fine. A finding about a DIFFERENT defect in the same file or function is NOT the same issue. Severity or aspect differences of the same root cause ARE the same issue.


For THIS scoring pass, duplicate equivalence is stricter than sharing a root cause.
You must compare the COMPLETE MATERIAL CLAIMS, including mechanism, triggering
conditions, execution path, and consequence. The same line or broad concern does
not establish equivalence. A report of wrong-category selection, a case/rename
mismatch, a crash, and a silent fallback are different claims even at one lookup.
An inactive/unbound API concern and an alleged active user-facing failure differ.
A compound report with an additional material claim does NOT equal its subset.
Differences only in wording, severity, or hedging do not create separate claims.
If the claimed mechanisms, triggers or consequences conflict, or one report adds
an unsupported/different material factual claim, return same=false. You are NOT
verifying which claim is true; do not repair or reinterpret either report to make
them match. If unsure whether their full claims are equivalent, return false.

For every numbered pair, extract what A and B actually CLAIM into mechanism,
trigger and consequence. Then list material_differences and give your equivalence
verdict, confidence and reason. same=true requires no material differences.
Return ONLY this JSON object, with EVERY pair index exactly once:
{"pairs":[{"pair":1,"a":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"b":{"mechanism":"...","trigger":"...","consequence":"..."},"material_differences":[],"same":true,"confidence":0.9,"reason":"..."}]}

A: The check `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` after parseRefreshTokenResponse is dead code, because parseRefreshTokenResponse already throws on failure; the Promise.reject branch can never execute. Not a behavior bug today, but it misleads readers into thinking there is a non-throwing failure path here; when someone later 'simplifies' parseRefreshTokenResponse to return results instead of throwing, this path silently becomes the only guard — and the mixed success-check/throw contract across callers (zoom checks .success, google uses .data directly) is itself a drift hazard.

PAIR 13:
A: refreshOAuthTokens POSTs calcomUserId and appSlug to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT with no authentication header, signature, or shared secret, so the sync endpoint can only hand out a user's OAuth access tokens to unauthenticated callers. Anyone who can reach the configured sync endpoint (e.g. an internet-reachable sync route on the parent cal.com deployment) can POST calcomUserId=<n> for arbitrary n and receive that user's fresh access token, harvesting credentials across all users by id enumeration; the diff's own webhook direction authenticates with a shared-secret header, but this direction sends nothing the endpoint could authenticate.
B: The outbound POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId`/`appSlug` with no authentication (no secret header, unlike the reverse webhook direction which requires `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`) — either the endpoint is unauthenticated (any caller can retrieve any user's credentials) or every sync call will 403

PAIR 15:
A: The inline contract for the sync endpoint — "The response should only contain the access token and expiry date" — contradicts what this diff's consumers actually require: Lark's handleLarkError demands the Lark envelope {code, msg, data}, Google/Hubspot/Zoho need provider-native objects (and crash per the shape findings), and Zoom/O365/Webex/Teams each parse their app-native token bodies. A parent-app implementer who builds to the documented contract gets an endpoint that works for none of the apps: lark-calendar sync permanently fails in handleLarkError on the bare {access_token} body, with an error that gives no hint the response shape is the problem; the real per-app contract exists only in each consumer's error handler.
B: The shipped payload contract is bespoke: the comment instructs deployers to "Customize the payload based on what your endpoint requires", i.e. edit this file, because the feature only works for parent apps whose endpoint accepts exactly calcomUserId+appSlug form-encoded and returns the unspecified token JSON. Any parent app whose API differs forces self-hosters to patch Cal.com source and re-merge on every upgrade — the feature is incomplete as shipped and the response field names (expiry_date vs expires_in vs Lark's nested envelope) are undefined, so no single endpoint response can satisfy all ten integrated apps.

PAIR 17:
A: The sync-endpoint fetch has no timeout/AbortController and no fallback to the local refreshFunction when the endpoint fails or hangs. A slow or hung parent endpoint stalls every calendar and video operation for the nine wired apps for the fetch's default timeout window with no degradation path, where the pre-PR code refreshed directly against the provider — one flaky self-hoster endpoint takes down all bookings that touch those apps.
B: The fetch to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT has no AbortSignal timeout, so a hung parent sync endpoint stalls the token-refresh path with no bound. Calendar availability and booking operations that need a token refresh block for up to the platform's default idle timeouts (minutes) per call whenever the parent cal.com endpoint is slow or down, turning a remote outage into local request stalls on the booking path.
